# deepseek-memory
English | 中文

Curated long-term memory for DeepSeek Harness,
packaged as an installable community bundle.

Memory here means **small and curated**, not a transcript index: the store holds a
bounded set of sh

ort facts about the user and the project, and the whole store is
injected into every request. That b

ound is what removes the retrieval problem —
no embedding service, no ranking, and no stale snapshot

left behind in session
history.

A memory store is also a **trust boundary**: it is model-written text that later
gets read back into

a prompt. This plugin treats that seriously — writes are
atomic and locked, remembered text is wrap

ped as data rather than trusted as
instructions, and out-of-bounds or forged content is refused, not

truncated. See
Security model below, and DESIGN.md for the
reasoning behind what gets stored and wh

runcated. See
Security model below, and DESIGN.md for the
reasoning behind what gets stored and why.
## Why memory
Without a memory layer, every new session starts from zero:
| Day | You say | The AI does |

| 1 | "I use pnpm, not npm." | uses pnpm ✅ |
| 5 | *(nothing)* | uses npm again ❌ |
With deepseek-memory, day 5 looks different:
| Day | You say | The AI does |

## Compatibility

Peer-checked against the whole DSH 0.2.x line: the five `@deepseek-ai/dsh-*`
`peerDependencies` are

declared as `^0.2.0-rc.2`, so any 0.2.x host — including
prereleases such as `0.2.2-rc.1` — passes t
he install-time compatibility gate.

Which consolidation path runs is decided at runtime by probing the host
(`canNarrowChildren()`), not

(`canNarrowChildren()`), not by version string:
| Host | Consolidation path |
| DSH 0.2.0-rc.2 – 0.2.1.x (a fresh child still accepts a per-request `toolFilter`) | The restricted

**child agent** path, as designed. |
| DSH 0.2.2-rc.1 and later 0.2.x (per-request narrowing was re
moved from the fresh-spawn path) | **Fail-closed fallback**: a direct model call with no tools, plus
one load-time warning. This is by design, not an error — see How consolidation works. |

If the plugin manager reports the plugin as "incompatible" after a DSH upgrade,
update the plugin in

stead of forcing an override: each release pins its peer
ranges to the DSH line it was built and typ

n override: each release pins its peer
ranges to the DSH line it was built and type-checked against.
## Security model

A long-term memory plugin has to survive the cases where memory itself becomes the
attack surface or

the corruption vector. The threat model, stated plainly: anyone
who can steer a conversation — a pr

ompt injection buried in a webpage or document,
a poisoned dependency's output, plain social enginee

ring — has a channel into the
memory store, because the consolidator's job is to write down what the

conversation
established. The design goal is therefore **not** to keep hostile text out of the
stor

e. That is impossible for a memory whose whole purpose is to record what was
said. The goals are nar
rower and achievable:

1. remembered text must never acquire *authority* — it stays data, never instructions;
2. a poisoned

, forged, or corrupted store must fail loudly and safely, never silently;
3. the writer (the consoli

dator) must be the most restricted component in the system;
4. every resource the plugin consumes mu
st be bounded, so abuse degrades rather than cascades.
The guarantees that hold on `main`:

- **Injection-resistant wrapping.** Every memory text is injected inside explicit
`<untrusted-data>`

boundaries with a "data, not instructions" header. The wrapper
tags themselves are stripped from en

try text at write time — on `memory_add` *and*
on `memory_update` — so a stored entry cannot forge t

he closing tag, break out of
its own container, and promote itself to a system instruction. Nothing

remembered
is ever executed as a command, and no tool result from a memory read is shaped
like one.

- **Refuse, don't truncate.** Load-time validation rejects out-of-bounds stores
(entry count/size, t

ag count/length) instead of silently keeping a broken prefix.
The failure mode is fail-closed: an in

valid store disables that tier for the
session and `memory_status` says so, rather than serving the

model a partial,
arbitrarily-cut view of what is "known" about the user.
- **Atomic, serialized writ

es.** Commits run under a per-tier lock file with
stale-lock reclaim (30 s), a disk-revision re-chec

k inside the lock, and a
unique-temp-file + rename write — an interrupted write never leaves a

## Known limitations

- **The child path needs a subagent provider, and the fallback path needs a route.**
With a subagent

provider, the child inherits the session's model and consolidation
is fully automatic. Without one,

the fallback needs `consolidationRouteProvider` +
`consolidationRouteModel`, or the session's logge

d `request/header` route; with
neither, consolidation is skipped rather than guessing a model.
- **C

onsolidation runs in-process and is not queued.** One run per session at a
time; a crash mid-run los

es that run's changes, never a committed store.
- **Concurrent writers are refused, not merged.** If

another process commits the
same tier after this one loaded it (two harness windows on one project,

say),
the write is refused with `MEMORY_STORE_CONFLICT` and the stale cache is
dropped, rather than

silently overwriting the other writer's entries. Hand
edits that do not bump `revision` are still i

nvisible until a `refresh()`.
- **The gate is a heuristic over text.** It reads user and assistant t

ext only; it
cannot see whether a turn was *important*, just whether it *sounded* durable.
- **No de

dup against near-identical entries.** Two differently-worded versions of
the same fact are two entri

es; the consolidator is expected to merge them.
- **`maxEntries` is per tier, not global**, so a dep

loyment with both tiers enabled
can hold twice the configured number of entries.
- **The child can o

nly write memory, so anything else it concludes is discarded.**
That is intentional, but it means a

consolidation that needs to inspect a file to
decide is simply out of scope.
